ea-gh-spirit-formed-and-returns.reason: Who shaped it is answered in section two, but where it goes waits until THE SPIRIT RETURNS TO HIM mid-lesson; the honest-identity payoff is in MADE BY HIM IS ENOUGH; ends on a discussion prompt.
ea-gh-spirit-formed-and-returns.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who shaped your spirit, and where does it go? Yahweh, who stretched out the heavens, forms the spirit within you (Zechariah 12:1), and when the body returns to dust, the spirit returns to Him who gave it (Ecclesiastes 12:7). So your honest identity is a creature at both ends: not only matter that switches off, and never a spark of deity. You are made, entrusted and going home. Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-spirit-formed-and-returns.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who shaped your spirit, and where does it go? Yahweh formed it, gave it understanding like a candle that carries His flame, and will receive it back, as Jesus committed His spirit into the Father's hands. That is a creature's honest identity: real, precious and made, never a god within. It frees you from manufacturing a self or proving your worth. Your spirit is on loan from Him and accountable to Him, and made by Yahweh is the highest thing that can be said of you.

teen.open: Who made your spirit, and where does it go when you die? Yahweh made it, and it goes back to Him. You are not just a body, and you are not a little god either.
teen.close: So you don't have to invent yourself or prove you matter. Yahweh made you on purpose, your spirit belongs to Him, and it goes home to Him.

senior.open: The title asks who shaped your spirit and where it goes. Zechariah 12:1 and Ecclesiastes 12:7 answer together: Yahweh forms the spirit within, and at death it returns to Him who gave it.
senior.close: So our identity is creaturely at both ends, formed by Him and returning to Him. That truth is not small; it is our dignity, and it means we live as stewards of a spirit entrusted to us.

ea-gh-eyes-opened-by-prayer.reason: Title asks if you must see the unseen to be unafraid; the answer (no: Elisha was calm before seeing, we walk by faith) waits until ELISHA ALREADY KNEW near the end; ends on a discussion prompt.
ea-gh-eyes-opened-by-prayer.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Do you need to see the unseen to be unafraid? No. Elisha was calm before his servant ever saw the chariots of fire. He already knew who was with them, because Yahweh had said so. The unseen realm is real, it is created and under Yahweh's rule, and when anyone saw it in this story, it was shown by Yahweh, never seized by method. Courage comes from trusting Him, not from sight. Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-eyes-opened-by-prayer.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Do you need to see the unseen to be unafraid? Elisha did not. His servant needed his eyes opened, but Elisha was at peace before anything was shown, because they that were with them were more than they that were against them (2 Kings 6:16). So you never have to chase sight by ritual or bargain for it. Walk by faith, not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7), stand in Yahweh's strength and armour, and pray. The chariots are there whether you see them or not.

teen.open: Do you have to see angels or the spiritual world to stop being scared? No. Elisha was calm before anyone saw anything, because he trusted Yahweh.
teen.close: So you don't need to see it to be brave. Yahweh's help is there whether you see it or not. Trust Him, pray, and don't go chasing the unseen.

senior.open: The title asks whether we must see the unseen to be free of fear. Elisha's calm answers it: he was at peace before his servant's eyes were opened, because he trusted what Yahweh had already said.
senior.close: So courage does not wait on sight. The unseen is real and under Yahweh's rule; sight, when He grants it, is His gift, never our technique. We walk by faith, and His presence is enough.

ea-gh-break-generational.reason: Yahweh's verdict (the son shall not bear the father's iniquity; the one who sees and turns breaks it) is clear in the first two sections; the lesson ends on a family discussion prompt.
ea-gh-break-generational.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Does the pattern stop with you? It can. Yahweh said the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father (Ezekiel 18:20), so a family pattern has no legal claim on the one who turns. Ezekiel names how the break happens: the son sees his father's sins, considers them, and does not do the same (Ezekiel 18:14). Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-break-generational.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Does the pattern stop with you? Yes, when you do what the son in Ezekiel did: see it, consider it, and do not do the same. Hezekiah and Josiah did it. In Christ you are redeemed from the empty way handed down from your fathers, and you are a new creature. So name the pattern, take it to the Word, and end its run in your generation. Yahweh's mercy reaches to thousands of generations of those who love Him, and what you plant runs forward.

teen.open: Do you have to repeat what your family has always done? No. Yahweh says each person answers for himself, and anyone who sees the pattern and turns can break it.
teen.close: So the pattern can stop with you. Name it, take it to the Word, and choose differently. Then pass on something good.

senior.open: The title asks whether a family pattern can stop with you. Ezekiel 18 answers yes: the son shall not bear the father's iniquity, and the one who sees, considers and does not do likewise breaks the line.
senior.close: So a family's past need not be your future. Like Hezekiah and Josiah, you can see the pattern and turn; in Christ you are a new creature, and what you plant can bless generations after you.

ea-gh-potter-shepherd.reason: The answer (clay does not design or fix itself; the making and the keeping are both His) is in the opening and THE POTTER'S HOUSE; the lesson ends on a clay activity prompt.
ea-gh-potter-shepherd.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can clay choose its shape? No. Clay does not design itself, and when it is marred it does not fix itself; the Potter does (Jeremiah 18:4). Isaiah says we are the clay and Yahweh is our Potter (Isaiah 64:8), and Peter says the strays are brought back to the Shepherd and Bishop of their souls (1 Peter 2:25). The making and the keeping are both His. Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-potter-shepherd.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can clay choose its shape? It cannot, and that is good news. The Potter knows the shape He intends, remakes what is marred, and will perfect what concerns you. Your part is to stay soft on the wheel, because resisting only makes the shaping longer and harder. You do not have to invent an identity; you receive the one your Maker intended. And when you wander, you do not find your own way back. You turn, and the Shepherd is already seeking you.

teen.open: Can you design who you are all by yourself? Not really. Yahweh is the Potter and we are the clay. He shapes us and keeps us.
teen.close: So you don't have to invent yourself. Stay soft and let Yahweh shape you. If you wander off, turn back, because He is already looking for you.

senior.open: The title asks whether clay can choose its shape. Isaiah 64:8 answers no: we are the clay and Yahweh is the Potter, and 1 Peter 2:25 adds that He is also the Shepherd who keeps our souls.
senior.close: So our identity is received, not invented. The Potter finishes His work in us when we stay yielded to His hands, and the Shepherd watches over and restores us all our days.

ea-gh-tithe-windows.reason: First section answers it (elsewhere Scripture forbids testing Yahweh; here He invites it); ends on a family discussion prompt rather than the invitation, and what the blessing is waits until mid-lesson.
ea-gh-tithe-windows.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Can you test heaven with your own budget? In this one place, yes. Elsewhere the Word forbids putting Yahweh to the test, but in Malachi 3:10 He invites it: bring the whole tithe into the storehouse and prove Him, and see if He will not open the windows of heaven. The test is not a way to buy favour or get rich. It is putting Him first with the first tenth, then watching Him provide. Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-tithe-windows.example: THE FIRST LINE, NOT THE LAST. Say a household brings home $4,000 a month. Before the rent, before savings, before any spending, the first line of the budget reads $400, given cheerfully to the storehouse. Everything below that line is planned from the $3,600 that remains. That order is the whole test. It says with the budget itself that all $4,000 was Yahweh's first, and it leaves room to watch what He does with the windows of heaven, the devourer and the month.
ea-gh-tithe-windows.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can you test heaven with your own budget? Yahweh says you can, in the tithe, and only there does He invite it. Acknowledge that all of it is His, set apart the first tenth before anything else, bring it to the storehouse cheerfully, and pair it with justice, mercy and faith. The blessing may be money, or provision in a crisis, a protected harvest and all sufficiency in all things. Take Him at His word: prove Him, and watch what He does.

teen.open: Can you actually test Yahweh with your money? In the tithe, yes. In Malachi 3:10 He says to give the first tenth and see if He doesn't pour out a blessing.
teen.close: So give the first tenth first, not what's left over, and give it gladly. Yahweh invited the test, so take Him at His word and watch Him provide.

senior.open: The title asks whether we may test heaven with our budget. Malachi 3:10 is the one place Yahweh invites it: bring the whole tithe into the storehouse and prove Him by it.
senior.close: So the tithe is the household's standing test of His faithfulness. Given first, cheerfully, and joined with justice, mercy and faith, it acknowledges that all is His and opens the way to His sufficient provision.

ea-gh-return-return.reason: The opening section states the answer (return unto Me, and I will return; the move is ours first and He is faithful); the lesson then ends on a family discussion prompt.
ea-gh-return-return.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why is the move yours first? Because Yahweh never moved. He does not change (Malachi 3:6); the distance came from our drift, a little at a time. So His word is simple: return unto Me, and I will return unto you (Malachi 3:7). One turn toward Him, today, opens the way back, however far the drift went, and He is faithful to His side of it. Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-return-return.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why is the move yours first, and what does one turn open? The distance was never His slowness; it was our heading. So when you turn, you find what the prodigal found: the Father saw him a great way off, ran to him, and met him with a robe, a ring and a feast before his speech was done. No probation, no long rehabilitation, no lock to pick. Draw near to Yahweh and He draws near to you (James 4:8). Make the one turn today.

teen.open: Feel far from Yahweh? He didn't move away from you. He says, return to Me and I will return to you. Your turn toward Him opens the way back.
teen.close: So don't wait until you've cleaned yourself up. Turn toward Yahweh today. Like the father in Jesus' story, He runs to meet you.

senior.open: The title says the move is ours first. Malachi 3:6-7 explains why: Yahweh does not change, the distance came from our drifting, and His promise is that when we return to Him, He returns to us.
senior.close: So the way back is one honest turn, made today. Yahweh is faithful to His side; His mercies are new every morning, and every morning is a morning to return.

ea-gh-no-weapon.reason: The opening two sections answer it (the attack is expected, but no weapon formed shall prosper; failure is inherited); the lesson ends on a discussion prompt instead of the heritage.
ea-gh-no-weapon.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Attacks are coming. Do they get to win? No. Isaiah 54:17 does not promise that no weapon will be formed against you; it promises that no weapon formed shall prosper, and that every tongue rising against you in judgment you shall condemn. The attack is expected; its failure is inherited. That is the heritage of Yahweh's servants, and their righteousness is from Him. Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-no-weapon.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Attacks are coming. Do they get to win? They do not. Haman hanged on his own gallows, the lions' mouths were shut for Daniel, and the accuser is answered not by your perfection but by Yahweh's cleansing and Christ's intercession. So expect opposition without fearing it. Keep building with the tool in one hand and the sword in the other, do what is right without panic, and answer every accusing tongue with the righteousness He has given you. The weapon will be formed. It will not prosper.

teen.open: People will come against you sometimes. Do they get to win? No. Yahweh says no weapon formed against you will succeed.
teen.close: So don't panic when attacks come. Keep doing what's right and trust Yahweh. The attack is real, but it won't win.

senior.open: The title asks whether the attacks that come must win. Isaiah 54:17 answers no: weapons will be formed, but none formed against Yahweh's servants shall prosper, and that protection is their inheritance.
senior.close: So we need not be surprised or shaken by opposition. We keep to our work, answer accusation with the righteousness Yahweh supplies, and rest in the heritage He has given His servants.

ea-gh-word-void.reason: The opening rain picture answers it (His Word shall not return void), sharpened in IT ACCOMPLISHES WHAT HE PLEASES; the lesson ends on a discussion prompt, not the promise.
ea-gh-word-void.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Does Scripture still work when you cannot see the harvest? Yes. Yahweh says His Word is like rain that does not go back to the sky empty but waters the earth and makes it bud. His Word shall not return to Him void; it accomplishes what He pleases and prospers in what He sent it to do (Isaiah 55:11), whether its fruit shows in a moment or decades later. Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-word-void.example: A VERSE WITH NO RECEIPT. Say a father reads one psalm aloud at breakfast every school morning for years, and his daughter mostly seems to be eating her cereal. He never sees a sign it landed. Years later, in a hard night far from home, a line from that psalm comes back to her, word for word, and steadies her. No one ever reports it to him. By Isaiah 55:11 the seed did its work all the same.
ea-gh-word-void.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Does Scripture still work when you cannot see the harvest? It does, because its power was never in the sower. The Word that framed the worlds turned Nineveh with one sentence and raised dry bones, and it endures when all flesh withers like grass. It may comfort or convict, now or twenty years from now, but it never returns empty. So keep sowing it into children, notes and conversations, stop measuring by visible results, and leave the harvest to Yahweh, who promised.

teen.open: Does reading or sharing the Word matter if you never see anything happen? Yes. Yahweh says His Word never comes back empty. It always does what He sent it to do.
teen.close: So keep reading it, memorizing it and sharing it, even when nothing seems to happen. The seed is working. The harvest is Yahweh's job.

senior.open: The title asks whether Scripture still works when we cannot see the harvest. Isaiah 55:10-11 answers that His Word, like the rain, never returns void but accomplishes what He pleases.
senior.close: So we may sow the Word without demanding a report. Its fruit may come quickly or long after we are gone, but it endures for ever and does exactly what He sent it to do.

ea-gh-known-before-formed.reason: Answered plainly in the second section (Jeremiah did not earn his calling; it was given before his first breath); the lesson closes on a discussion prompt rather than the settled identity.
ea-gh-known-before-formed.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Did you have to earn your purpose? No. Yahweh told Jeremiah that before He formed him in the belly He knew him, set him apart and ordained him (Jeremiah 1:5). All of it came before Jeremiah's first breath. He did not earn his calling by proving himself; it was recognized, not manufactured. Paul says believers too were called not by their works but by His own purpose and grace (2 Timothy 1:9). Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-known-before-formed.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did you have to earn your purpose? You did not. You were known before you could perform, and your worth was settled before your first success or failure. That makes it stable: circumstances cannot un-choose what was chosen before they existed. So stop auditioning and stop saying, I am a child, when Yahweh has called. Ask what you were made for, and walk in the good works He prepared, as Jeremiah, Moses and Gideon did, carried by His promise: I am with thee.

teen.open: Do you have to prove yourself to get a purpose? No. Yahweh told Jeremiah He knew him and had a plan for him before he was even born.
teen.close: So you don't need to earn your worth. Yahweh knew you first. Instead of asking if you're good enough, ask what He made you for, and go do it with Him.

senior.open: The title asks whether we must earn our purpose. Jeremiah 1:5 answers no: Yahweh knew, set apart and appointed him before he was born, and He calls believers by His purpose and grace, not their works.
senior.close: So our worth rests on being known before we could perform, which no circumstance can undo. We still labour, as Jeremiah did, but from settled identity and the promise of His presence, not from anxious striving.

ea-gh-end-from-beginning.reason: Implied from the start, but the plain answer (Yahweh has already written and published the last chapter) waits for THE LAST CHAPTER IS ALREADY PUBLISHED near the end; ends on a discussion prompt.
ea-gh-end-from-beginning.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who writes the last chapter of history? Yahweh does, and He has already written it. In Isaiah 46 He says He declares the end from the beginning, and His counsel shall stand. The idols cannot tell what is coming; only He can, because He purposes it and brings it to pass. So the ending is not in doubt, however chaotic the middle looks. Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-end-from-beginning.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who writes the last chapter of history? Yahweh, who told the crushing of the serpent in the garden, named Bethlehem centuries early, and held even the cross inside His determinate counsel. He has published the end: He will dwell with His people, wipe away all tears, and make all things new (Revelation 21:3-5). No rival can rewrite that page. So live from the ending, not the headline. Peace does not come from knowing every detail of tomorrow; it comes from knowing who wrote the last page.

teen.open: Who decides how the whole story of the world ends? Yahweh does. He told the ending before it began, and what He plans happens.
teen.close: So when the news is scary, remember who wrote the last page. Yahweh already told us the ending: no more tears, everything made new.

senior.open: The title asks who writes the last chapter of history. Isaiah 46:9-10 answers that Yahweh alone declares the end from the beginning, and His counsel shall stand.
senior.close: So the ending is secure in His hand, already declared in Revelation 21. That certainty steadies us in the confusing middle of history and of our own lives.

ea-gh-first-and-last.reason: Opens on the First-and-Last titles; the plain answer (your past is not out of His reach, your future not unknown to Him) only arrives in section four; ends on a discussion prompt.
ea-gh-first-and-last.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is your worst yesterday or your scariest tomorrow outside Yahweh's reach? Neither one is. He is the First and the Last (Isaiah 44:6), and the risen Jesus takes the same name (Revelation 1:17). He stands at both ends of time at once, so no moment of your life is behind Him or ahead of Him. Your past is not out of His reach, and your future is not unknown to Him. Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-first-and-last.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is your worst yesterday or your scariest tomorrow outside Yahweh's reach? No. He is Lord of yesterday: He does not erase history, but He redeems it and makes a way in the wilderness, with mercies new every morning. He is already standing in tomorrow: Jesus has gone ahead to prepare a place and holds the keys of death. So bring Him both, the regret and the dread. Every chapter of your life is held between the hands of the One who is, and was, and is to come.

teen.open: Is your worst mistake or your biggest worry too far for Yahweh to reach? No. He is the First and the Last. He is already in your past and your future.
teen.close: So hand Him the thing you regret and the thing you're scared of. He can redeem yesterday, and He is already waiting in tomorrow.

senior.open: The title asks whether our worst past or most fearful future lies beyond Yahweh's reach. He answers as the First and the Last, standing at both ends of time, so nothing behind or ahead of us is outside His hand.
senior.close: So neither regret nor dread has the final word. The One who began the story redeems our yesterdays and already holds our tomorrows; we may rest today in Him who is the same yesterday, today and for ever.

ea-gh-word-written-on-the-heart.reason: Both halves of the title (law written on the heart and conscience; renewing means agreeing with that witness) are answered only mid-lesson in THE CHOICE IS NOT and RENEW THE MIND; ends on a prompt.
ea-gh-word-written-on-the-heart.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why is Yahweh's law not a stranger to your conscience? Because He wrote on you first. Even those without the written law show its work written in their hearts, with the conscience bearing witness (Romans 2:15), and in the new covenant He writes His law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33). So renewing your mind does not ask you to learn a foreign rule. It asks your thinking to agree with what your heart already knows. Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-word-written-on-the-heart.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why is Yahweh's law no stranger, and what does renewing your mind really ask? The conscience is a witness He placed inside, which is why truth stings at first and then feels like coming home. Renewing the mind asks you to stop arguing with that witness: be honest about what you already know, feed your thinking the written Word daily, and keep your conscience tender instead of searing it. When the mind matches the heart, the war inside ends, and you have the peace of a Sound Mind.

teen.open: Ever notice your conscience already knows right from wrong? That's because Yahweh wrote His law on your heart. Renewing your mind means letting your thoughts agree with it.
teen.close: So don't argue with that inside voice when it lines up with the Word. Read the Word every day, listen to your conscience, and you'll have peace inside.

senior.open: The title says Yahweh's law is already written within us. Romans 2:15 and Jeremiah 31:33 show the conscience bearing witness to it, so renewing the mind means bringing our thinking into agreement with that inner witness.
senior.close: So the work of renewal is honesty with what we already know. Fed daily by the Word and kept tender, the conscience and the mind come into agreement, and integrity brings its quiet peace.

ea-gh-call-evil-good.reason: The answer (blurring a plain line is not fairness; false balance is under the same woe) sits in a heading and in THE FOG OF FALSE BALANCE mid-lesson; ends on a discussion prompt.
ea-gh-call-evil-good.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is blurring the line really being fair? No. Isaiah 5:20 puts a woe on those who call evil good and darkness light, and that includes the quieter move of laying a fog over a plain line so it only looks unclear. Treating a settled matter as forever open is not humility; it is false balance. Real fairness names plain truth as true and keeps uncertainty honest and narrow, where the Word is truly silent. Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-call-evil-good.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is blurring the line really being fair? It is not. A clear line exists, because Yahweh is light and in Him is no darkness at all. Calling darkness a shade of light falls under Isaiah's woe, and a person who keeps blurring the line slowly loses the ability to see it. Real fairness says yes and no plainly where the Word has spoken, stays honest where it is silent, and does it with the humility of the forgiven. Walk as a child of light, and the people who listen to you will have somewhere to stand.

teen.open: Is it fair to act like right and wrong are just a gray area? Not when the Word is clear. Yahweh warns those who call evil good.
teen.close: So be kind, but be clear. Where the Word speaks plainly, say yes or no. Blurring the line isn't fair; it just leaves people with nowhere to stand.

senior.open: The title asks whether blurring a plain line is fairness. Isaiah 5:20 answers no: those who call evil good and darkness light stand under a woe, and fog over a settled matter is the same failure in a quieter voice.
senior.close: So fairness and moral clarity are not enemies. We name good and evil as the Word does, stay honest where it is silent, and keep the line with humility, as children of light.

ea-gh-peace-peace.reason: The heading and A REAL WOUND answer it early (treating a real wound slightly does not heal it, it abandons the wounded); the lesson ends on a discussion prompt.
ea-gh-peace-peace.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is saying it's fine really healing? No. Jeremiah 6:14 condemns leaders who healed the hurt of the people slightly, saying peace, peace, when there was no peace. They did not deny the wound; they put a light bandage on it and announced it was fine. Declaring a real wound healed does not heal it. It abandons the wounded and keeps the real cure from being applied. Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-peace-peace.example: TWO ANSWERS TO ONE HURT. Say a teenager tells a parent that a friend group has been cruel to her for months. One answer is, it's fine, kids are like that, don't overstate it. The conversation ends quickly and the parent feels better, but the girl is left alone with it. The other answer is the Samaritan's: sit down, look at the hurt honestly, name it, and do something about it together. The first soothes the observer. The second binds up the wound.
ea-gh-peace-peace.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is it's fine really healing? It is not. Slight healing is whitewash on a cracked wall: it looks sound until the storm comes. Jeremiah asked whether there was no balm in Gilead, and the tragedy was that a cure existed but the wound had never been named honestly enough to use it. Real love does what the Samaritan did and what Yahweh does: it sees the wound, names it gently and truly, and binds it up. Speak the truth in love, and the real cure can begin.

teen.open: When something is really wrong, does saying it's fine fix it? No. Jeremiah 6:14 warns against covering a real hurt with easy words.
teen.close: So don't brush off real pain, yours or anyone else's. Name it honestly and kindly, and bring it to Yahweh. That's how healing actually starts.

senior.open: The title asks whether saying it's fine is real healing. Jeremiah 6:14 answers no: treating a genuine wound slightly, with comfortable words, leaves it untended and keeps the true cure from being applied.
senior.close: So the kinder act is the honest one. Naming a real hurt plainly and in love, as the Samaritan did, opens the way for Yahweh's full healing, which He never applies slightly.

ea-gh-credit-vs-worship.reason: The opening defines credit vs worship, but who gets the glory (credit traces to Yahweh who gives the power; worship is His alone; people get honest thanks) is spread over four sections; ends on a prompt.
ea-gh-credit-vs-worship.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who gets the glory for what you built? Separate two debts. Credit is owed for what was done, and it traces back to Yahweh, who gives you the power to get wealth (Deuteronomy 8:18); people who truly worked deserve honest thanks along the way. Worship is owed for who someone is, and it belongs to Yahweh alone; He will not give His glory to another (Isaiah 42:8). Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-credit-vs-worship.example: FINISHING THE SENTENCE. Say a woman opens a bakery and, five years in, it is thriving. Honest credit sounds like this: I worked early mornings, my husband kept the books, and a mentor taught me pricing. Then she finishes the sentence: and Yahweh gave the hands, the health, the years and the open door. She thanks the people by name. But she does not organise her life around the bakery, the mentor, or her own discipline. The throne stays His.
ea-gh-credit-vs-worship.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who gets the glory for what you built? Thank the people who truly worked, because honest credit is not idolatry. Then trace the chain up: what do you have that you did not receive (1 Corinthians 4:7)? Yahweh supplied the capacity, so the credit was never only yours, and worship belongs to Him alone. Self-credit and creature-worship are the same mistake, glory on the wrong object. Not unto us, but unto His name, and your heart keeps only one throne.

teen.open: When you do something great, who gets the glory? Thank the people who helped you, but remember Yahweh gave you the ability. Worship belongs only to Him.
teen.close: So say thank you to the people who helped, and then thank Yahweh who gave you everything you worked with. Keep Him alone on the throne of your heart.

senior.open: The title asks who gets the glory for what we build. The Word separates two debts: credit traces back to Yahweh who gives the power to get wealth, with honest thanks to human helpers, while worship is His alone.
senior.close: So we may honour real work in real people without confusion, because all we have was received. The glory belongs to Yahweh, who will not give it to another, and success is remembered rightly when we remember who gave it.

ea-gh-inscription-that-asked-eternity.reason: The answer (the priest's carved plea went silent; the Word of Yahweh and of Jesus is still read today) is only stated in TWO CLAIMS, SIDE BY SIDE, the third section; ends on a discussion prompt.
ea-gh-inscription-that-asked-eternity.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Which words are still being read today? Not the priest's. At Philae he carved an inscription asking to last for all time and eternity, and within a few generations no one living could read it. The words still being read are the Word of Yahweh and the words of His Son: the grass withers, but His Word stands for ever (Isaiah 40:8), and Jesus said His words shall not pass away (Matthew 24:35). Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-inscription-that-asked-eternity.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Which words are still being read today? Lay the two claims side by side. The words carved in stone by a man who asked for ever went silent for some fourteen centuries. The words spoken about grass and flowers, and by a Teacher on a hillside, are quoted this morning in hundreds of languages. The Word does what it says and gives new birth. So anchor what you want to endure in it: your hours, your teaching, your legacy. It has the words of eternal life.

teen.open: A priest carved words in stone asking them to last forever, and soon nobody could read them. Which words are still read today? Yahweh's Word.
teen.close: So build your life on what lasts. Stone fades and people forget, but Yahweh's Word is still being read everywhere, and it gives real life.

senior.open: The title asks which words are still being read. The priest's inscription at Philae, which asked for eternity, lost its readers; the Word of Yahweh and the words of Jesus, which promised to stand for ever, are read still.
senior.close: So the comparison settles where our hopes belong. Every carved monument withers like grass; the Word endures and makes alive those who receive it. What we plant in it, and in the people it births, will last.

ea-gh-justice-rationed-at-the-gate.reason: Why bought justice is wrong (filed among mighty sins) and what Yahweh says (He pleads the poor man's cause) are split across sections three to six; ends on a discussion prompt.
ea-gh-justice-rationed-at-the-gate.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why shouldn't justice cost a fortune, and what does Yahweh say about the poor man's case? In Israel the gate was the courthouse, and Amos files turning the poor aside there among the people's mighty sins (Amos 5:12). When justice must be bought, only the rich get it, and the poor man's case never even arrives. Yahweh's answer is twofold: establish judgment in the gate, and where it stays shut, He pleads their cause Himself (Proverbs 22:23). Here is how the Word shows it.
ea-gh-justice-rationed-at-the-gate.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why shouldn't justice cost a fortune? Because Yahweh counts a shut courthouse door as a mighty sin, not a side effect. His law aims its commands at the powerful: take no gift, respect no person, wrest no poor man's judgment. So measure justice by whether the poor man's case arrives, not only by whether the law is written fairly. Speak for the one who cannot, and if you are the one shut out, keep coming like the widow. Yahweh pleads your cause, and you have an Advocate who does not bill.

teen.open: Should only rich people be able to get justice? No. Yahweh calls shutting the poor out of court a serious sin, and He promises to plead their case Himself.
teen.close: So stand up for people who can't be heard. And if you're the one shut out, keep praying and keep coming. Yahweh is on the side of the poor.

senior.open: The title asks why justice should not cost a fortune and what Yahweh says of the poor man's case. Amos names turning the poor aside at the gate a mighty sin, and Proverbs 22:23 says Yahweh will plead their cause.
senior.close: So a justice system is judged by whether the poor are actually heard. We use whatever standing we have to speak for those without it, and those shut out may keep coming, for the Judge of all the earth hears them.
